title: Companions on the road
hook: the Zohar's sages walk the roads of Galilee, teaching as they go

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shechinah: the presence that dwells among the people, at a table, and even in exile. Your line was presence dwells. Did you notice the space between you and someone? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-one.

Two rabbis are walking on a road. Dust, heat, hills, a long way still to go. One of them says to the other: let's open our mouths with words of Torah, so the walk isn't wasted. An old man trudges along with them, driving a donkey. A hired hand, as far as they can tell. Then the donkey driver starts to talk, and out of his mouth come teachings that leave the two rabbis astonished. The Zohar, a central book of Kabbalah, tells scenes like this. Here, the teaching doesn't happen in a hall. It happens on the road. Today's words.
screen: `TWO RABBIS ON A ROAD.` → `A DONKEY DRIVER BEHIND THEM.` → `TEACHING THAT HAPPENS WALKING.`

segments.voice: Companions on the road. In Aramaic, the Zohar calls them the chevraya, the companions. Turn it four ways. First, who they are. Tradition ties the Zohar to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, a sage of the Mishnah, and the book tells of him and his circle walking the roads of the land of Israel, Galilee and beyond, teaching as they go. Scholars ask hard questions about when the book was written, and there are different answers. Either way, inside the book, this is the scene: friends, walking, talking Torah. Second, why the road. Yesterday's teaching was that when people sit together and their talk is Torah, the Shechinah rests among them. The Zohar's companions carry that onto the road. In the Zohar, sages say that when travelers speak words of Torah, the presence joins them on the way. A road becomes a moving sanctuary. Third, the stranger. More than once in the Zohar, the teacher turns out to be someone the companions overlooked: an old donkey driver, a child, a traveler on the road. The scene teaches its readers to stay open, because wisdom may be walking just behind them. Fourth, companionship itself. In these stories, nobody learns alone. One companion asks a question, another answers, a third sees something new in the answer. Rabbi Shimon praises them when they get it right. The secrets of the Torah, in this picture, open up between people, in conversation, on the way somewhere. The book itself teaches like a walk with friends.
screen: `THE CHEVRAYA, THE COMPANIONS.` · `TORAH ON THE ROAD.` · `THE STRANGER WHO TEACHES.` · `NOBODY LEARNS ALONE.` · then, large: `COMPANIONS ON THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk and talk with a friend. For now, settle, and breathe. Think of one person you'd like to walk beside, a friend, a sibling, someone you've lost touch with. Picture the road: where you'd go, what the ground would feel like. Then think of one real question you'd want to ask them, something worth the walk. Not small talk. Something about what matters to them. Hold the question and the face together. Later today, if you can, take that walk, or make that call while you walk. The bell holds the time.
Companions on the road. The chevraya of the Zohar: friends walking together, teaching Torah as they go, and finding wisdom in strangers. Today's words.
Your line: companions on the road. Today, walk somewhere with one person, or call one while you walk, and ask them the question you held. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: The Zohar is often studied in pairs or small circles, reading aloud together, and some study groups take walks or journeys to sites in Galilee linked to its sages.

original.note: Aramaic: the companions, the Zohar's name for Rabbi Shimon's circle.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pleasant picture of friends on a walk.
what it means: in the Zohar, teaching happens on the road, between companions, with the presence walking alongside.
what a scholar hears: the chevraya of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, the road as a setting for revelation, and the old donkey driver of the Zohar on Mishpatim (Saba de-Mishpatim).

notes: Saba de-Mishpatim (Zohar 2:94b ff.): Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Yose meet an old donkey driver who turns out to be a great sage. The hook's scene blends this with the Zohar's common opening ('rabbis walking on the road, let us open with words of Torah'); please confirm and check the folio.

'Again and again in the Zohar, the deepest teacher turns out to be someone the companions overlooked' (donkey driver, child, traveler): a frequency claim without a count; the child refers to the Yanuka passages. Please confirm or soften.
'Scenes like this fill the Zohar' and 'the great book of Kabbalah' are characterizations, not superlatives from the text; please confirm.

Authorship: tradition ties the Zohar to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai; the teach says only that scholars ask about its date and give different answers. Modern attribution (Moses de León, 13th-century Castile) deliberately left out under the claims rule.
Original: חֶבְרַיָּא vocalization and pronunciation; please confirm.
